title: Mira and the Grumpy Gate
markdown:
Mira adjusted her goggles, the dappled sunlight of Dr. Quill’s garden warming her face. Rosemary and old books perfumed the air; a bee had opinions about the rosemary. Beside her, Sol the fox waited, his tail a soft rhythm on the cool earth. They had come for a mysterious metal gate at the garden’s far end, grand with squirrels and vines in the ironwork, streaked with grumpy red-brown that had not been in last month’s sketch.

Sol twitched his nose. “It looks like a grumpy old man who forgot to wash his face. And it smells dusty, like a damp book.”

Mira touched a gritty, rough patch. The metal snagged. “It’s falling apart.” She had expected gleam. She found a crumbling puzzle. A fleck flaked off like mud. Rubbing only made the rust spread, a pinkish smear on her glove.

Dr. Imani Quill arrived, silver hair a blur, already pulling on work gloves that had seen worse gates. “The Gate of Grumbles. It seems to have brought its own charm.”

Mira’s brow furrowed. “It looks left out in the rain for years, not just arrived. The metal feels weak.”

Quill smiled. “Notice the colour. The texture. Feel it again, but listen with your fingers.”

Mira leaned closer, a faint metallic scent. The reddish-brown was a creeping blush along the vine-scrolls, worst where rain would sit. The rough grit whispered decay — not a secret, a fact you could hear as a scrape. The air seemed a gentle artist, painting layer by layer, and the gate had not consented.

“The air is tickling it. Turning it red and scratchy.”

“A good observation. The air is full of invisible things. Oxygen, for iron, is an eager friend. It wants to combine. A chemical reaction.”

Mira pictured tiny oxygen sprites and then, because she was an apprentice engineer, pictured molecules that did not need faces. “So the air is making friends with the gate.”

“In a way. When iron meets oxygen, especially with a little water, it changes. That reddish-brown stuff is rust. Iron combined with oxygen. Oxidation.”

“Oxidation. The air is oxidizing the gate, and that makes it rust.”

“This iron is susceptible. We need to slow it so it doesn’t crumble.”

Mira’s mind whirred. “If oxygen is the problem, put something between air and metal. Stop them meeting.”

“Thinking like an engineer. What could you use as a shield?”

She spotted a pot of clear sealant on the potting bench, lid stubborn, smell sharp. She applied it to a small section of scrollwork. Instantly the metal darkened, shone, grit vanished under a skin that felt like a decision.

“Smooth again. A little raincoat for the metal.”

Sol sniffed the sealant. “It smells a bit like that. But the metal looks less grumpy. Perhaps a happy smell for the metal.”

Quill patted her shoulder. “A shield. Paint would do. Zinc, if we get fancy, to keep that eager oxygen from making rust-cake.”

Mira looked at the gate, no longer only a puzzle. She coated another wet-prone dip, then a third, working from the worst blush outward so the rain would have less to drink. Sol sat on the sealant lid so it would not roll into the rosemary.

She did not ask the sky what other everyday mysteries were waiting. She wrote oxidation / water / barrier in her notebook, dated the patch test, and left the Gate of Grumbles looking, if not cheerful, at least as if someone had finally washed its face.
